extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for performing Section 101 patent-eligibility analyses (judicial exceptions: abstract ideas, laws of nature/natural phenomena, and products of nature), with special focus on identifying and evaluating nature-based products via the markedly different characteristics analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract idea — mathematical formulas and related concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical formulas (e.g., Arrhenius equation) and similar concepts are judicial exceptions (abstract ideas) and thus non‑statutory subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize mathematical formulas and related information‑processing concepts as abstract ideas (citing Diehr, Benson, Flook, Mackay, Bilski). Examples include algorithms for binary conversion (Benson), formulas for alarm limits (Flook), electromagnetic standing wave formulas (Mackay), and mathematical formulas for hedging (Bilski). If a claim is directed to such an abstract idea, it is a judicial exception (Step 2A: YES) and requires further Step 2B analysis to determine whether the claim recites a patent‑eligible application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concepts relating to performing mathematical calculations
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that are directed to generating/manipulating data by performing mathematical calculations are abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that consist of calculating values, manipulating results, organizing information via mathematical correlations, or otherwise performing mathematical computations should be treated as abstract ideas (examples: Bancorp, Digitech). Include algorithmic examples (In re Maucorps, In re Grams, In re Abele). Use the specification to determine whether the claimed steps are mere mathematical computation or tied to a practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws of nature and natural phenomena — general rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws of nature and natural phenomena (naturally occurring principles/relations and nature‑based products that are naturally occurring or not markedly different from what occurs in nature) are judicial exceptions to patent eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The basic tools of scientific/technological work (laws of nature, scientific principles, natural phenomena, products of nature) are not patentable. Examples include isolated DNA, cloned animals, correlations between biomarkers and disease, electromagnetism for transmission, and naturally occurring chemical principles (citing Funk Bros., Chakrabarty, Myriad, Mayo, etc.). If a claim recites a law of nature or natural phenomenon, treat it as a judicial exception (Step 2A: YES) and proceed to Step 2B to examine whether the claim recites a patent‑eligible application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Products of nature — when a claimed product is an exception
rubrics_metrics.description: When a law of nature or natural phenomenon is claimed as a physical product, it is treated as a 'product of nature' exception if the product is naturally occurring or lacks markedly different characteristics from a natural counterpart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Products of nature include both naturally occurring products and human‑made products that are structurally identical to natural counterparts. Examples: isolated DNA (Myriad), primers (Ambry), cloned animals (Roslin). Non‑naturally occurring products are not automatically eligible simply because of human intervention; the key is whether they possess markedly different characteristics from any naturally occurring counterpart.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markedly different characteristics analysis — purpose and outcome
rubrics_metrics.description: The markedly different characteristics analysis (part of Step 2A) determines whether a claimed nature‑based product is a product of nature exception by comparing claimed product characteristics to its natural counterpart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the nature‑based product has markedly different characteristics (structure, function, and/or other properties) from its natural counterpart, then the limitation is not a product of nature exception and the claim is not directed to a product of nature (Step 2A: NO) unless another exception is present. If it does not exhibit markedly different characteristics, the limitation is a product of nature (Step 2A: YES) and further Step 2B analysis is required to determine eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to perform the markedly different characteristics analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the markedly different characteristics analysis only to nature‑based product limitations in the claim; avoid extending it to non‑nature‑based aspects of the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The analysis should be performed when the claim recites a nature‑based product (either alone or as a limitation). Do not apply the analysis to claims or claim elements that are not nature‑based. If the claim is to a single nature‑based product, analyze the entire product; if the claim includes additional elements, analyze only the nature‑based product limitation for markedly different characteristics and evaluate additional elements under Step 2B if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product claims — apply analysis to the entire claimed product
rubrics_metrics.description: For claims directed to a nature‑based product itself (e.g., 'a Lactobacillus bacterium'), apply the markedly different characteristics analysis to the entire product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare the claimed product as a whole to the naturally occurring counterpart (citing Chakrabarty). If the claimed product as claimed exhibits markedly different characteristics, it is not a product of nature; otherwise it is and Step 2B follows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination (multi‑component) nature‑based product claims — analyze the resultant combination
rubrics_metrics.description: When the claim is to a nature‑based combination produced by combining components (e.g., a probiotic composition of Lactobacillus and milk), analyze the resultant combination rather than component parts separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the mixture or combined product as claimed has markedly different characteristics from any naturally occurring counterpart. The closest counterpart to a claimed combination may be the resultant combination (if it occurs in nature) or the individual components when no counterpart mixture exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims reciting a nature‑based product plus non‑nature elements
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim includes a nature‑based product limitation in combination with non‑nature elements (e.g., container, instructions), perform the markedly different characteristics analysis only on the nature‑based product limitation; evaluate other elements in Step 2B if the nature‑based product is a product of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For example, for a 'yogurt starter kit comprising Lactobacillus in a container with instructions', analyze Lactobacillus for markedly different characteristics. The container and instructions are not part of the markedly different characteristics analysis but may be considered as additional elements when assessing whether the claim recites significantly more (Step 2B). Cite Funk Bros. as an example where only the bacterial mixture was analyzed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product‑by‑process claims — focus on product characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: For product‑by‑process claims, the analysis depends on whether the claimed nature‑based product has markedly different characteristics from its natural counterpart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether the claimed product (regardless of the process language) exhibits markedly different characteristics; consult MPEP § 2113 for additional product‑by‑process guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process claims — generally focus on active steps, not product characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Process claims are generally not subject to the markedly different characteristics analysis for nature‑based products used in the process because the focus is on the process steps rather than products used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the claimed process itself is directed to a patent‑ineligible product or merely to the use of nature‑based products. If a process claim is drafted so it is indistinguishable in substance from a product claim (e.g., 'a method of providing an apple'), then it may be subject to the markedly different characteristics analysis and treated as directed to the product (citing Rapid Litigation Mgmt. v. CellzDirect and Ariosa/Sequenom).

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting appropriate natural counterpart(s)
rubrics_metrics.description: Select the closest naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state for comparison when performing the markedly different characteristics analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the nature‑based product is derived from a natural thing, use the thing from which it was derived as the counterpart (e.g., deoxyacid A derived from acid A). Do not conflate the counterpart with adjacent natural material (e.g., compare an isolated gene to the gene, not the whole chromosome). Where multiple natural counterparts exist, select the closest based on expertise (e.g., donor/sheep breed). For combinations with no natural counterpart, compare to the individual components as appropriate (citing Chakrabarty, Roslin, Funk Bros., Ambry). If rejecting on eligibility grounds, best practice is to identify the selected counterpart in the Office action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying and evaluating characteristics for 'markedly different'
rubrics_metrics.description: Markedly different characteristics can be expressed as differences in structure, function, and/or other properties, and must be evaluated based on what is recited in the claim on a case‑by‑case basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare the claimed nature‑based product's recited structure, function, and properties to the natural counterpart in its natural state. If the claimed limitation is naturally occurring, no analysis is necessary because it is directed to a naturally occurring product by definition. For non‑naturally occurring limitations created by human intervention, perform the comparison to determine whether the claimed characteristics are markedly different.

rubrics_metrics.name: BRI and amendment recommendation best practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI), a nature‑based product limitation may encompass both eligible and ineligible embodiments; examiners should point out BRI issues and recommend narrowing amendments where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim's BRI would encompass embodiments that are products of nature and embodiments that have markedly different characteristics, treat the claim as directed to a product of nature (Step 2A: YES) and, if rejecting under Step 2B for lack of inventive concept, it is best practice to identify the BRI and recommend claim amendments to narrow the claim to eligible embodiments when possible (citing Roslin).
